description: I’m building TRACE (Tracking Regional Atmospheric Change on Earth) as a solo project for NASA Space Apps. The app uses 25 years of NASA POWER data to show how temperature, precipitation, or sunlight reaching Earth’s surface has changed worldwide.
summary: TRACE (Tracking Regional Atmospheric Change on Earth) is an open web atlas for the Be An Earth System Trend Detective! challenge. It analyzes NASA POWER (MERRA-2) temperature and precipitation from 1981 to 2024 across 54,425 land grid cells between 60°S and 84°N. Users can search 223 countries or select a single cell to see what changed, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. TRACE then asks a question a significance test cannot answer: is the change real? It screens each record for abrupt jumps that can imitate a gradual trend, and it cross-checks the result against a second record: NASA GISTEMP v4 for temperature and GPCP v2.3 for precipitation. Worldwide, land warmed about 0.25 °C per decade in MERRA-2 and 0.35 °C per decade in GISTEMP. In Bangladesh, MERRA-2 reports significant cooling of −0.19 °C per decade, driven by a jump around 1997, while station records show warming of +0.35 °C per decade. Students, educators, and analysts can retrace every calculation, share the exact view, and download the evidence.
details:
TRACE is a global trend detective for near-surface air temperature and precipitation. The World view colors every land cell from 60°S to 84°N by its 1981–2024 trend, by a single year (with playback), by its 1991–2020 normal, or by a verdict layer that shows whether an independent record supports the trend there. Users can search any of 223 countries or click one cell. TRACE then builds that area’s annual series, estimates its trend per decade with a 95% interval, tests significance, screens for discontinuities, and compares the result with a second record over exactly the same footprint. Every view lives in the URL so it can be shared, and every selection can be exported with its area, trend, uncertainty, method, and limits. Seven countries (Bangladesh, Chile, Kenya, Mexico, Morocco, the Philippines and Spain) also have seven-variable packs that add daily maximum and minimum temperature, root-zone soil wetness, relative humidity, and wind speed.

The method is designed for autocorrelated climate records. TRACE uses monthly NASA POWER MERRA-2 data on its native 0.5° × 0.625° grid, converts it to anomalies against the WMO 1991–2020 normal (rainfall as a percentage of each cell’s own normal), and weights each cell by its true land area. Theil–Sen estimates the rate of change with a Gilbert confidence interval. Mann–Kendall tests significance with the Hamed–Rao correction for serial correlation. Benjamini–Hochberg controls false discoveries across 54,425 tests per variable at a 10% target rate. A BIC comparison between a straight line and a single step flags records where an abrupt jump explains the data better than a trend. TRACE then cross-examines the result against NASA GISTEMP v4 land-station temperatures and GPCP v2.3 satellite-and-gauge precipitation. For trends that are not yet significant, it estimates how many more years of data would be needed at the current rate and noise.

The global results show why that second look matters. Land warmed about 0.25 °C per decade in MERRA-2 (95% interval 0.19–0.31) and 0.35 °C per decade in GISTEMP (0.29–0.40), and 71% of land is selected as warming after false-discovery control. Station records back that warming on about 59% of land. TRACE flags 4.8% of land as a likely data artefact for temperature and 13.5% for precipitation. Of the 141 countries large enough to compare, 100 are corroborated by stations and 7 are flagged as likely artefacts, including Bangladesh, Honduras, Nicaragua and the Philippines. Across South Asia, the station records mostly lean the opposite way to the reanalysis.

Four guided case files reach four different outcomes, so readers learn that significance is not the same as truth. In central Chile, both precipitation records confirm a post-2010 drought (−17.1% versus −11.2% of normal per decade): corroborated. In Chile’s coast and Andes, daytime highs diverge (−0.01 versus +0.29 °C per decade), but the 2° comparison grid is wider than the country: no witness at this scale. In Bangladesh, MERRA-2 shows significant cooling of −0.19 °C per decade with temperature, humidity, and soil moisture all jumping around 1997–98, while GISTEMP shows +0.35 °C per decade: a likely data artefact. In Kenya, both records show warming at different rates (+0.18 versus +0.34 °C per decade): same direction, different size.

TRACE is built for people who need to check climate claims before acting on them. Students, educators, and researchers can explore any country or cell without building a data pipeline. NASA data teams can use each disagreement as a repeatable case for quality review. Public agencies can examine warming or rainfall evidence, including its uncertainty and assumptions, before it goes into an adaptation assessment. TRACE is an evidence-screening prototype. It does not forecast, attribute causes, or replace a local risk model, and institutional adoption has not yet been demonstrated. The two precipitation records share some rain-gauge inputs, the comparison grids are coarser (2° and 2.5°), and neither record is ground truth. Agreement adds support. Disagreement tells users where to look closer.

The data pipeline is written in Python (numpy, shapely, netCDF4). It tiles about 700 NASA POWER requests, reads the comparison records, and packs the results into compact binaries. The statistics engine is written in TypeScript and shared by the build scripts and the browser, so the published headlines and the interactive results always agree. A separate Python implementation (scipy, pymannkendall) recomputes every national headline and a sample of global cells, and continuous integration fails if the two disagree. The interface uses React, Astryx, D3, and WebGL, rendering a rotating globe over NASA GIBS Blue Marble relief. The site is static and open source under Apache 2.0, and it runs without an account, API key, or backend.
